explainedBy: In the cozy conference room the boss talks warmly while the peripheral colleague sinks back: the social pull to belong at work.

storyboard.claim: What happens in the warm conference room is a subconscious social dynamic.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The dissenting colleague slumping quietly while the smiling CEO holds the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the conference room from the shared/unshared information setup.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who holds back (the peripheral colleague) and who sets the mood (the boss).

explainedBy: The mechanism starts: the desire to belong to the tribe is the cause of what follows.

storyboard.claim: We survive by belonging, so people suppress contradictory information to fit in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow begins with its first cause: desire to belong.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the room into the mechanism behind it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the cause of suppression as a structure.

explainedBy: Desire to belong leads to staying quiet: nobody wants to be the squeaky wheel that ruins the vibe with the leader.

storyboard.claim: People keep the bond with the leader and avoid being the squeaky wheel.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains its second step: stay quiet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the effect of the desire to belong.
storyboard.addedInformation: Cause -> behaviour now visible.

explainedBy: The chain ends: belonging -> staying quiet -> the most valuable unique information is buried.

storyboard.claim: The most valuable unique information is buried by our desire to be liked.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow completes with its result: best info buried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the result to the chain.
storyboard.addedInformation: The full cause -> effect chain of the conformity trap.

explainedBy: The hidden profile stays hidden unless a different voice speaks up: the peripheral colleague talks and the boss is surprised.

storyboard.claim: The only known antidote to the conformity trap is diversity, not as a buzzword.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The colleague from a different background speaking up while the CEO reacts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the trap to its cure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cure as the outsider voice actually speaking.

explainedBy: The empirical example comes from a courtroom: social psychologist Samuel Sommers's jury research.
noVisual: Sommers is not in the cast; the law icon and court set carry the jury setting, his name rides on the callout.

storyboard.claim: Johnson highlights social psychologist Samuel Sommers's experiments.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A courtroom with the law icon; Sommers's name.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the general claim to a measured example.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: sets up the jury context; the name is text.

explainedBy: Sommers set up dozens of mock juries to deliberate a complex case, varying who sat on them.

storyboard.claim: Sommers gave dozens of mock juries a complex case and manipulated their composition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The court stage kept; the callout names the mock juries.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept court stage; the label moves from the man to the method.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: method is text-carried; the court keeps it a jury.

explainedBy: The experiment's two conditions side by side: homogeneous all-white juries versus racially diverse juries.

storyboard.claim: Some juries were all white; others mixed white and Black jurors.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter with the two jury types.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Splits the experiment into its two groups.
storyboard.addedInformation: The comparison the whole experiment rests on.

explainedBy: Result: in the diverse jury, a Black juror and a white juror deliberating together did vastly better at critical thinking.

storyboard.claim: By every metric the diverse juries performed vastly better.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two clearly different jurors deliberating in court.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the outcome of the two-group comparison.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the winning group as mixed people actually deliberating.

explainedBy: What 'better' meant, part one: the diverse juries debated longer, and it was not just noise.

storyboard.claim: They did debate longer, but it wasn't just noise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter of findings starts: debated longer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins breaking down how they were better.
storyboard.addedInformation: First measured difference.

explainedBy: Part two: they remembered the specific facts of the trial transcript far more accurately.

storyboard.claim: They remembered the granular facts of the transcript far more accurately.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The findings sorter gains: remembered facts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the second finding.
storyboard.addedInformation: Second measured difference.

explainedBy: Part three: they entertained a much wider range of interpretations of the evidence.

storyboard.claim: They entertained a much wider range of interpretations; homogeneous groups settled on one narrative at once.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The findings sorter gains: wider interpretations.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the third finding.
storyboard.addedInformation: Third measured difference, completing the list.

explainedBy: In the homogeneous room the juror feels the warm consensus and stops thinking: he sits with a blank face.

storyboard.claim: Homogeneous groups felt warm consensus and clocked out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A juror sitting blank-faced, mentally checked out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the diverse findings with the homogeneous room.
storyboard.addedInformation: The face shows the stopping of thought.

explainedBy: In the diverse room the same white juror, next to a Black juror who talks, examines the evidence with a magnifier and makes fewer errors.

storyboard.claim: White jurors in diverse rooms made fewer factual errors than in all-white rooms.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The white juror scrutinizing evidence beside the Black juror.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same juror as 201, now in a diverse room and engaged.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the presence of the other juror changing his effort.

explainedBy: Diversity raised everyone's thinking: both jurors now engaged, the white juror holding the lightbulb of understanding.

storyboard.claim: The diversity elevated everyone's cognitive baseline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Both jurors engaged and pleased, a lightbulb in hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From fewer errors to the general lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the lightbulb stands for sharper thinking.

explainedBy: Applied to daily life: the listener drawing up the invite list for a team to launch a product.

storyboard.claim: If you form a team at work or an HOA board and only invite people like you...
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener holding a list of whom to invite.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the jury study to the listener's own life.
storyboard.addedInformation: The invite list makes the choice of members concrete.

explainedBy: Inviting only people with the same college, class or jargon leads straight to flying blind.

storyboard.claim: Choosing only people with your background means actively choosing to fly blind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: same background -> flying blind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the consequence of the invite list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Cause -> effect as a structure.

explainedBy: The chain ends: a homogeneous jury for your own choices guarantees hidden profiles stay hidden.

storyboard.claim: You build a homogeneous jury for your life and guarantee hidden profiles stay hidden.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains its result: profiles stay hidden.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the final consequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the application back to the hidden-profile idea.

explainedBy: The listener pushes back as devil's advocate: theory is great, practice is messy.

storyboard.claim: Devil's advocate: theory is great, but practice is messy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener raising a skeptical objection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from argument to objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the objection is mostly text.

explainedBy: Adding outsiders makes the meeting drag on: the clock beside a weary team member.

storyboard.claim: Adding outsiders makes meetings drag on for an extra hour.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A clock beside the listener slumping in a long meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First cost of the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clock shows the lost time.

explainedBy: The friction in the room: the boss gets defensive and points angrily at the dissenting colleague.

storyboard.claim: It makes people defensive and creates interpersonal conflict.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The CEO angrily pointing at the dissenting colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second cost: the conflict itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who gets defensive and at whom.

explainedBy: Having your core assumptions challenged is unpleasant: the colleague speaks and the boss sags under it.

storyboard.claim: Yes, it creates friction; having your core assumptions challenged is rarely pleasant.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The colleague talking while the CEO slumps, uncomfortable.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reverses roles from 209: now the boss is on the receiving end.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the discomfort of being challenged.

explainedBy: When someone disagrees with your worldview you feel discomfort: the colleague points and the listener feels it.

storyboard.claim: The friction is the entire point; that discomfort is your brain being pushed out of a mode.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The colleague disagreeing, the listener uncomfortable.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the friction as the purpose.
storyboard.addedInformation: The discomfort is visible on the listener.

explainedBy: Kahneman's two modes as a scale: the marker sits at System one, the fast intuitive autopilot.

storyboard.claim: Kahneman's System one is our fast intuitive autopilot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum System one <-> System two, marker on System one.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mode the discomfort pushes us out of.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows where we start on the scale.

explainedBy: The dissenting voice forces the brain to shift gears: the marker moves to System two, slow and analytical.

storyboard.claim: The discomfort of dissent shifts the brain into System two: deliberative, analytical.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The marker slides over to System two.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Marker moves from one pole to the other.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shift of gears is the visible change.

explainedBy: Cause and effect: the social discomfort of diversity jolts groupthink to a halt.

storyboard.claim: The social discomfort of diversity jolts groupthink to a halt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: social discomfort -> groupthink halted.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the gear shift into the group effect.
storyboard.addedInformation: Cause -> effect as structure.

explainedBy: It acts as a speed bump: the easy flawed cognitive shortcut is blocked, so the discomfort is the medicine.

storyboard.claim: It is a speed bump that prevents the easy flawed shortcut; the discomfort is the medicine.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains: shortcut blocked.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the final effect.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes why discomfort helps.

callout.text: Only ever lived in one place

explainedBy: A room full of people with the same experience cannot map a complex world: the confident boss alone talking.
noVisual: No map icon in the vocabulary; the narration's map metaphor rides on the callout.

storyboard.claim: You cannot draw an accurate map of a complex world with a room of people from one place.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The confident boss talking, no other voice present.
storyboard.onScreenText: Only ever lived in one place
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the argument as a metaphor.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the map metaphor is text-carried.

explainedBy: To see the whole terrain you embrace the friction: the boss now lets the different voice speak.

storyboard.claim: Embrace the friction; widen the map before you choose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The colleague speaking while the CEO listens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the closed room in 216 to one that includes the outsider.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows widening as letting the other voice in.

explainedBy: Having mapped the present, the next step is the future: the listener walks toward the horizon.

storyboard.claim: With the terrain mapped and hidden profiles exposed, the next step is the future.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener walking toward the horizon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition from mapping to predicting.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the horizon stands for what lies ahead.

explainedBy: Prediction is where experts fail hardest; the story returns to the analyst in the 2011 White House deliberations.

storyboard.claim: Prediction is where experts fail; back to the White House Situation Room in early 2011.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The CIA analyst, weighed down by the coming prediction.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the Abbottabad case from the everyday application.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the date is text; the analyst re-anchors the case.

explainedBy: The analysts present their findings to the President's cabinet around the scale model of the compound.

storyboard.claim: The analysts present their mapped findings to Obama and his cabinet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The analyst presenting beside the compound model.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the signature object back.
storyboard.addedInformation: The model makes 'the case being presented' concrete.

explainedBy: Growing confidence: the analyst points at the courtyard of the model where the tall man paces.

storyboard.claim: They grow confident the tall man pacing the courtyard is bin Laden.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The analyst pointing at the model, now confident.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept model; the analyst moves from presenting to pointing with confidence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the confidence and its focus: the compound courtyard.

explainedBy: The room tilts toward a strike, but John Brennan pushes back at the analyst beside the model, refusing to ride the consensus.

storyboard.claim: The room tilts toward a strike, but John Brennan refuses to ride the wave of consensus.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brennan sternly pointing at the analyst beside the model; she is taken aback.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept model; Brennan enters and confronts the confident analyst.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who resists and against whom.
